title: A node dies at 03:14
subtitle: The timeline, second by second, and why one pod never moves
scenario:
node3 loses power. It was running six pods: four from a Deployment, one from a DaemonSet, and `postgres-0` from a StatefulSet with a PersistentVolume.

Nobody is awake. Follow what the cluster does on its own, and find the one pod that will still be stuck when you wake up.

steps.title: The node stops talking

ask.prompt: What does the control plane actually stop receiving?
choices: The kubelet's Lease renewal in kube-node-lease, which it writes every 10 seconds
A heartbeat from kube-proxy on that node
The full NodeStatus update, which is sent every second
A TCP keepalive from the scheduler to the node
ask.explain: Node liveness is a tiny Lease object renewed every 10s, kept deliberately separate from the much heavier NodeStatus (every ~5 min). Splitting them is what let clusters grow past a few hundred nodes without hammering etcd.

steps.body:
The kubelet on node3 was renewing a `Lease` object every 10 seconds. The power cut stops it mid-cycle.

Nothing happens yet. The control plane has no idea — a missed renewal is indistinguishable from a slow network for the first few seconds, and reacting instantly to that would make every brief blip an outage.

code.label: the heartbeat that stopped
code.text:
$ kubectl -n kube-node-lease get lease node3 -o jsonpath='{.spec.renewTime}'
2026-05-02T03:14:07.000000Z

$ date -u
2026-05-02T03:14:31Z          # 24 seconds of silence so far

steps.title: The node controller gives up waiting
steps.body:
After `--node-monitor-grace-period` (40 seconds by default), the node controller inside kube-controller-manager marks node3 `NotReady`.

Look at the conditions carefully: they say `Unknown`, not `False`. That distinction is worth memorizing. `Unknown` means silence — the kubelet is not reporting at all, so go look at the machine. `False` would mean the kubelet is alive and telling you what is wrong.

At the same moment, the node is tainted `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute`. That taint is the eviction timer starting.

code.label: silence versus a complaint
code.text:
$ kubectl describe node node3 | grep -A6 Conditions:
  Type             Status    Reason               Message
  MemoryPressure   Unknown   NodeStatusUnknown    Kubelet stopped posting node status
  DiskPressure     Unknown   NodeStatusUnknown    Kubelet stopped posting node status
  Ready            Unknown   NodeStatusUnknown    Kubelet stopped posting node status

$ kubectl get node node3 -o jsonpath='{.spec.taints}'
[{"key":"node.kubernetes.io/unreachable","effect":"NoExecute","timeAdded":"..."}]

steps.watch: Meanwhile, on node3 itself, nothing is running at all — but if this had been a network partition rather than a power cut, the kubelet would still be happily restarting crashed containers from its local cache.

steps.title: Five minutes of nothing, on purpose

ask.prompt: The node is unreachable and tainted NoExecute. Why do its pods not get evicted immediately?
choices: Every pod carries a default 300-second toleration for that taint, so brief partitions do not cause mass churn
The scheduler has no spare capacity yet
Eviction waits for the node object to be deleted
The kubelet must confirm the eviction, and it cannot be reached
ask.explain: Admission adds `tolerationSeconds: 300` for unreachable and not-ready to essentially every pod. It is the cluster's judgment that five minutes of tolerance beats rescheduling the world every time a switch reboots.

steps.body:
The pods are tainted-out but tolerate it for 300 seconds. So for five minutes the cluster does nothing, deliberately.

If this were a switch reboot rather than a dead machine, node3 would come back in that window and nothing would have moved. That is the trade being made: slower failover in exchange for not thrashing on every blip.

You can shorten it per workload — but on a flaky network you will pay for it with churn.

code.label: faster failover, if you really want it
code.text:
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable
    operator: Exists
    effect: NoExecute
    tolerationSeconds: 30          # default is 300
  - key: node.kubernetes.io/not-ready
    operator: Exists
    effect: NoExecute
    tolerationSeconds: 30

steps.title: The Deployment pods are replaced
steps.body:
The toleration expires and the pods are marked for deletion. They go to `Terminating` and stay there, because the kubelet that would confirm the deletion is gone.

But the ReplicaSet controller does not wait for that. It counts Ready pods, sees 4 wanted and 0 healthy, and creates replacements. The scheduler places them on the surviving nodes and they start.

This is the part people get wrong in conversation: nothing is *migrated*. The old pods are not moved. New pods are created from the same template, with new names and new IPs.

code.label: recreated, not moved
code.text:
$ kubectl get pods -l app=api -o wide
NAME                   READY   STATUS        NODE
api-6b8f9c-2xk9p       1/1     Terminating   node3    # ghost, waiting for a dead kubelet
api-6b8f9c-hh4tz       1/1     Running       node1    # brand new
api-6b8f9c-m2p8w       1/1     Running       node2

steps.watch: A bare pod — one with no controller — is simply gone. Nothing recreates it. That is the real argument against `kubectl run` in production.

steps.title: The DaemonSet pod does not come back

ask.prompt: What happens to node3's DaemonSet pod?
choices: Nothing is created elsewhere — a DaemonSet runs one pod per node, and there is one fewer node
It is rescheduled onto node1, which now runs two
It stays Pending until node3 returns
The DaemonSet controller reduces its desired count and reports degraded
ask.explain: DaemonSets are indexed by node, not by replica count. Losing a node means losing that node's copy, and nothing anywhere else should compensate. Its DESIRED number simply drops.

steps.body:
The DaemonSet's desired count drops from 3 to 2, matching the surviving nodes. There is nothing to replace.

This is also why DaemonSet pods carry very broad tolerations — including for unreachable and not-ready nodes. Infrastructure like the CNI must be able to run on a node that is NotReady, otherwise a node could never recover its networking: the CNI is a pod, and the node stays NotReady until the CNI is running.

code.label: the count follows the fleet
code.text:
$ kubectl -n kube-system get ds rke2-canal
NAME         DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
rke2-canal   2         2         2       80d      # was 3

steps.title: And postgres-0 does not move at all

ask.prompt: `postgres-0` from a StatefulSet is Terminating on the dead node. Why is no replacement started?
choices: StatefulSet identity must be unique, and while the node is unreachable the control plane cannot prove the old pod is really gone
StatefulSets are not managed by controllers
The scheduler refuses to place pods with PersistentVolumeClaims
Its PodDisruptionBudget forbids it
ask.explain: Unreachable is not the same as dead. Starting a second `postgres-0` while the first might still be running and writing to the same disk is how you corrupt a database. Kubernetes chooses to stay stuck rather than risk it.

steps.body:
This is the pod that is still broken when you wake up.

A Deployment pod is interchangeable, so making another one is safe. `postgres-0` is not: there must only ever be one, and it owns a specific disk. From the control plane's point of view node3 is *unreachable*, not *confirmed dead* — and those are very different things when the wrong answer means two writers on one filesystem.

So it waits. Indefinitely.

code.label: stuck, and correctly so
code.text:
$ kubectl get pods -l app=postgres
NAME         READY   STATUS        NODE     AGE
postgres-0   1/1     Terminating   node3    21d      # forever, until you act

$ kubectl get pvc data-postgres-0
NAME              STATUS   VOLUME     CAPACITY
data-postgres-0   Bound    pvc-8a1f   100Gi        # still bound to the same disk

steps.title: And the disk is still attached to a dead machine
steps.body:
Even if the pod were replaced, the volume is a second obstacle. A ReadWriteOnce volume can be attached to exactly one node, and the cluster still believes it is attached to node3.

The attach-detach controller waits (about six minutes) before force-detaching, and on many storage backends that only fully resolves once the Node object is gone. Until then any replacement pod sits in `ContainerCreating` with `Multi-Attach error`.

code.label: follow the attachment
code.text:
$ kubectl get volumeattachment | grep pvc-8a1f
NAME       ATTACHER               PV         NODE    ATTACHED
csi-9f2a   csi.trident.netapp.io   pvc-8a1f   node3   true

$ kubectl describe pod postgres-0 | tail -3
  Warning  FailedAttachVolume  Multi-Attach error for volume "pvc-8a1f":
           Volume is already exclusively attached to one node and can't be attached to another

steps.title: The one decision that unsticks it

ask.prompt: You have confirmed node3's hardware is dead and will not return. What actually releases postgres-0?
choices: Deleting the Node object — that is the cluster's signal that the machine is really gone, releasing the pod and the volume attachment
kubectl delete pod postgres-0 --force --grace-period=0, on its own
Restarting kube-controller-manager
Deleting and recreating the PersistentVolumeClaim
ask.explain: Deleting the Node is you supplying the one piece of information the control plane could not get for itself: the machine is gone, nothing is running on it. That lets the pod be removed and the volume detached. Force-deleting the pod alone can leave the volume attachment behind — and if the node were only partitioned rather than dead, it would be exactly the double-writer scenario the system was protecting you from.

steps.body:
The whole stall is the cluster refusing to guess. You supply the fact it is missing.

Once the Node object is deleted, `postgres-0` is removed, the VolumeAttachment is released, and a fresh `postgres-0` is scheduled onto a surviving node, reattaching `data-postgres-0` — the same disk, the same data.

Before you type it, be certain. If the machine is actually alive behind a partition, you have just authorized a second writer.

code.label: the recovery, in order
code.text:
# 1. be sure. console, IPMI, hypervisor - not just ping
# 2. then:
$ kubectl delete node node3

$ kubectl get pods -l app=postgres -o wide
NAME         READY   STATUS    NODE     AGE
postgres-0   1/1     Running   node1    40s      # same PVC, same data

# if the node ever comes back, it re-registers as a fresh node

takeaways: The default timeline is ~40s to NotReady, then ~5 more minutes before pods are evicted. Roughly 5m40s to failover.
`Unknown` conditions mean the kubelet is silent — go to the machine. `False` means it is alive and telling you the problem.
Nothing is migrated. Controllers create replacements; DaemonSets simply have one fewer node to cover.
StatefulSet pods and ReadWriteOnce volumes deliberately stay stuck, because unreachable is not the same as dead. Deleting the Node object is how you tell the cluster which it was.
